newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SAS meets rising costs by trimming network.
newsitem.headline: SAS meets rising costs by trimming network.

text.p: Scandinavian airline SAS's cancellation of six international routes shows the carrier is having its wings clipped to keep up with competitive rival airlines, analysts said on Wednesday.

SAS plans next year to end services to Osaka in Japan from Stockholm and Copenhagen and routes from Copenhagen to Borlange in Sweden, to and from Newcastle, England, Lyon in France, Minsk in Belarus and Athens in Greece.
"These routes have too small a passenger base to allow them to operate with a profit," said SAS, which is partly owned by the governments of Sweden, Denmark and Norway.
Analysts had expected some cancellations as SAS last month said it would cut costs after a 41 percent slump in pre-tax profits to 1.26 billion crowns ($184 million) for the first nine months of 1996.
"If they don't follow pace with British Airways (BA) in terms of cuts, the planes may still be flying -- but at a big price," one Copenhagen-based analyst said.
SAS said it was open to cooperation with other carriers or its partners on the routes it plans to cancel.
"We would be interested in discussing possible cooperation on certain routes as we would like to safeguard transit traffic," SAS spokeswoman Marie Ehrling said.
Some analysts said Copenhagen-based SAS's alliance with Deutsche Lufthansa AG, which began in 1995, had not met expectations.

"The most disappointing news is Osaka. It shows the Lufthansa partnership is not providing SAS with the feeder traffic from northern Germany to Copenhagen," an analyst said. "It shows Frankfurt's strength."
Aviation analyst Bo Sehlberg, who produces an industry newsletter in Sweden, said SAS was set to become more of a feeder airline.
"They can still offer the service to Osaka for example without taking it out of the timetable because of the partnership with Lufthansa," he said.
SAS said it would concentrate more on Finland and add frequencies on routes to Karlstad, Sweden, and Dublin in Ireland.
From April 1 the airline would fly to Oulu, Finland, twice daily and double its frequencies to Finnish cities Tampere, Vaasa and Turku.

The route to Osaka would be cancelled from March 1. Changes in routes to Borlange, Newcastle, Lyon, France and Umea, Sweden, would take effect on April 1. The Athens route would be cancelled in the autumn of 1997.
No changes were announced to the carrier's cargo operations.
Rival carriers are, meanwhile, moving into domestic markets where SAS traditionally dominated.

Norwegian group Braathens SAFE recently snatched half of domestic Swedish airline Transwede with plans to buy the remaining 50 percent and expand its BA-linked frequent flyer programme to include Transwede flights.
Last month it also launched six daily flights between Oslo and Stockholm, one of SAS's most profitable routes.

British airline Virgin Express, which started flights between Copenhagen and Brussels this autumn, has said it is eyeing more routes in Scandinavia where it could add its no-frills, low-cost passenger flights.
In May BA linked with Danish carrier Sun-Air, under which Sun-Air's 260 weekly flights in Denmark and to Norway and Sweden would take BA codes.
($1=6.84 crowns)
